newsitem.title: KENYA: Summit on Sudan, Somalia opens without Museveni.
newsitem.headline: Summit on Sudan, Somalia opens without Museveni.

text.p: Leaders of five African states opened a summit in Nairobi on civil war in Sudan and Somalia on Tuesday but Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni's absence put real progress in doubt.
Kenyan officials said they had no idea why Museveni, who had pressed for the summit under auspices of the Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD), failed to arrive in Nairobi.

But a diplomat, who declined to be identified, told Reuters Museveni held that he would only attend if he could secure an agreement for the release of 21 schoolgirls abducted in October in northern Uganda by Ugandan rebels with bases in south Sudan.

The schoolgirls were abducted by the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), which Uganda says is backed by the government of Sudanese President Lieutenant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir, who attended the talks.
"Museveni holds he could not come to Nairobi unless he won the release of the schoolgirls. Attempts to persuade him to change his position and attend have failed," said the diplomat.
"Without Museveni, we cannot expect to achieve much."
Uganda was represented by First Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Eriya Kategaya at State House in Nairobi.
The summit was opened by Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi one day after nine people were killed during the most violent clashes between police and protesters in Kenya in seven years.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi, Eritrean President Isayas Afewerki and Djibouti President Hassan Gouled Aptidon also attended the talks, expected to end on Wednesday morning.

Opening the summit, Moi noted the last IGAD-sponsored meetings with Bashir and Sudanese rebel leader John Garang broke down in September 1994 as "one party was not in a position" to sign a declaration of principles as a basis for more talks.
The party which declined to sign was Sudan's government.
"The parties in the conflict should give serious thought to the declaration of principles and be willing to negotiate," said Moi, without referring directly to the Sudanese government.
"I wish to state here very clearly that I am not willing to continue chairing meetings if decisions being arrived at are not adhered to," Moi added in a warning his patience was running thin.
Moi noted that the civil war in southern Sudan had escalated to include eastern and northern Sudan, where an Eritrea-based rebel alliance has mounted several offensives since January.
"We must therefore bring the escalation of the conflict in eastern and northern Sudan to the forefront and find a quick solution by urging all parties in the conflict to pursue peace," Moi said.
He added the summit might also discuss the seven years of civil war in Somalia, which is a member of IGAD but has no internationally-recognised government so was not represented.
"Why should these problems (Sudan and Somalia) have been discussed for many years? These questions must be settled once and for all," added Moi in another sign of his frustration.
A Kenyan official said Kenya was not keen to retain the IGAD chairmanship, mainly because it was footing the bill for its meetings in Kenya. Moi urged member states to pay up for IGAD.
Garang's Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) has fought since 1983 for greater autonomy or independence for the Christian and animist south from the Moslem and Arabised north.

At talks hosted by Kenya in May, Bashir and Museveni agreed to release all those captured in border clashes. But the Ugandan leader has said he will not release more than 100 Sudanese prisoners unless Sudan helped secure the schoolgirls' freedom.
Uganda accuses Sudan's government of arming and giving bases in south Sudan to the LRA. Khartoum accuses Uganda of supplying and sending troops to fight alongside the SPLA in the south.
